title: ModuleNotFoundError
jokes: Python looked everywhere for '{module_name}' and found nothing, much like your test coverage.
'{module_name}' does not exist in this timeline. Try pip install.
You imported '{module_name}' on vibes alone. It did not work.
Congratulations, you've discovered a module that isn't installed: '{module_name}'.
Python's import system just ghosted you looking for '{module_name}'.
'{module_name}' is currently on a coffee break. Also it's not installed.
Bold of you to assume '{module_name}' would just be there.

gordon-ramsay: IT'S NOT INSTALLED! '{module_name}' IS RAW! You forgot to pip install it, you donut!
'{module_name}'?! I've seen better imports from a first-year cooking student!
zen: The module '{module_name}' does not yet exist in your environment. This too can be resolved.
Breathe. '{module_name}' simply needs to be installed. All is well.
sarcastic-senior-dev: '{module_name}' isn't installed. Yes, again. pip install exists for a reason.
Seen this one a thousand times: '{module_name}' is never installed on the first try.

fix.summary: Install the missing package.

title: IndentationError
jokes: Python is not a vibes-based indentation language. Fix your whitespace.
Tabs and spaces had a fight and your file lost.
Your code's indentation is more chaotic than your sleep schedule.
IndentationError: because Python cares more about whitespace than you do.
Somewhere, a tab and four spaces are locked in combat inside your file.
This isn't free-form poetry. Indent consistently.

fix.summary: Check for mixed tabs/spaces and re-indent consistently.

title: SyntaxError
jokes: Python couldn't parse that. Neither could I, honestly.
That's not Python. That's just vibes with parentheses.
SyntaxError: your keyboard may have slipped.
You wrote something Python has never seen before. Not in a good way.
This code compiles in the language of hope only.
Even the parser is confused, and it doesn't get confused.

fix.summary: Re-read the flagged line for a missing colon, paren, or quote.

title: NameError
jokes: '{name}' is not defined. Neither is your variable-naming strategy.
You used '{name}' before you created it. Time travel isn't supported.
Python has no idea what '{name}' is. Honestly, fair.
'{name}' sounds like something you meant to declare and forgot.
This is the Python equivalent of asking for someone who doesn't work here.
'{name}' is not defined, much like the requirements for this feature.

fix.summary: Define the variable before use, or check for a typo.

sarcastic-senior-dev: '{name}' is not defined. I'd ask if you meant something else, but I already know the answer is no.
Undefined name '{name}'. Every junior does this exactly once a day.

title: AttributeError
jokes: '{type_name}' does not have '.{attr_name}'. It never did. It never will.
You asked a '{type_name}' for '.{attr_name}' like it owed you something.
'.{attr_name}' is not real and cannot hurt you. Also it's not on '{type_name}'.
That '{type_name}' object looked at '.{attr_name}' and said 'never heard of her'.
AttributeError: you're calling a method that simply does not exist on '{type_name}'.
Someone assumed duck typing would save them. It did not.

fix.summary: Check the object type and available attributes.

sarcastic-senior-dev: '{type_name}' has no '.{attr_name}'. Did you check the docs, or just guess and hope?
That attribute doesn't exist on '{type_name}'. It never has. This isn't new information.

title: TypeError: argument mismatch
jokes: Wrong number of arguments. Math was always going to catch up with you.
You called a function like it was a suggestion box.
This function has opinions about how many arguments it accepts. Listen to it.
TypeError: you and this function disagree on arity.
Somewhere, a function signature is silently judging you.

fix.summary: Check the function signature and pass the correct number of arguments.

title: KeyError
jokes: '{key}' is not in that dict. It never checked in.
You reached into a dictionary for '{key}' and came up empty-handed.
KeyError: '{key}' — a classic tale of assuming data exists.
'{key}' is missing, much like input validation.
This dict does not recognize '{key}' as a member of this family.

fix.summary: Use .get() with a default, or verify the key exists first.

sarcastic-senior-dev: '{key}' isn't in that dict. A quick .get() with a default would've saved us both this conversation.
KeyError on '{key}'. Classic 'assume the data is always there' move.

title: IndexError
jokes: You reached past the end of the list. It ends where it ends.
IndexError: there is no spoon at that index.
That list is shorter than your ambitions.
You asked for an element that simply isn't there. Bold.
Off-by-one errors: the original sin of programming.

fix.summary: Check the list length before indexing.

title: ZeroDivisionError
jokes: You divided by zero. Math itself just filed a complaint.
ZeroDivisionError: the universe declines to cooperate.
Dividing by zero is how black holes start. Please stop.
Even your calculator wouldn't do this.
This is the one error message every language agrees on hating.

fix.summary: Guard the divisor with a zero check before dividing.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Division by zero. I've fixed this exact bug for three different interns this year.
You divided by zero. Add the guard clause. We both know you will, eventually.

title: ImportError: circular import

matcher.pattern: ImportError: cannot import name '(\w+)' from partially initialized module

jokes: '{name}' is stuck in a circular import loop with no way out.
Two modules are importing each other and now nobody wins.
This is an import ouroboros. It's eating its own tail.
'{name}' can't be imported because the module doing the importing is also being imported. Yes, really.
Circular imports: the Python equivalent of two people holding a door for each other forever.

fix.summary: Restructure imports to break the cycle, or move the import inside the function.

title: FileNotFoundError

matcher.pattern: FileNotFoundError: \[Errno 2\] No such file or directory: '([^']+)'

jokes: '{path}' does not exist. You may have imagined it.
Python looked for '{path}' with real dedication and found nothing.
'{path}' is a work of fiction as far as your filesystem is concerned.
That file is not there. It was maybe never there.
'{path}': 404, this path could not be found in real life.

fix.summary: Check the path is correct and the file exists relative to your working directory.

title: RecursionError
jokes: Your function called itself into oblivion.
RecursionError: it's recursion all the way down, then Python gives up.
You wrote a function that never wanted to stop calling itself.
This is what happens when you forget the base case.
Infinite recursion: technically a stack overflow with extra steps.

fix.summary: Add or fix the base case that should stop the recursion.

title: ValueError: invalid literal for int()

matcher.pattern: ValueError: invalid literal for int\(\) with base \d+: '([^']*)'

jokes: '{value}' is not a number. It never was.
You tried to make '{value}' into an int through sheer force of will. It didn't work.
ValueError: '{value}' remains stubbornly non-numeric.
int('{value}') was always going to fail.
'{value}' identifies as a string and Python respects that.

fix.summary: Validate the string is numeric before calling int(), or wrap in try/except.

title: PermissionError
jokes: Your OS just said no.
PermissionError: the filesystem does not trust you today.
You don't have permission for that. Neither does anyone else, apparently.
Access denied, in the most literal way possible.
The filesystem gods have rejected your request.

fix.summary: Check file permissions or run with the correct user/privileges.

title: SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'

matcher.pattern: SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'

jokes: You wrote Python 2. This is Python 3. Time has moved on.
print is a function now. It has been for over a decade.
This code was written for a Python that has already reached end of life.
SyntaxError: your print statement is a museum piece.
Somewhere, a Python 2 tutorial from 2011 is still doing damage.
You forgot the parentheses. print() called, it wants its function syntax back.

fix.summary: Wrap the print arguments in parentheses.

title: RuntimeError: This event loop is already running

matcher.pattern: RuntimeError: This event loop is already running

jokes: You tried to run an event loop inside an event loop. It's loops all the way down.
asyncio is already busy running things, and you just interrupted it rudely.
This event loop is already running, and it does not appreciate the company.
You called run_until_complete() from inside a coroutine. asyncio noticed.
Nested event loops: a bold move that asyncio will not allow.
The loop is already spinning. You cannot spin it again.

fix.summary: Avoid nesting event loops; await the coroutine directly instead of calling run().

title: RuntimeError: no running event loop
jokes: You called an async function like it was a regular one. asyncio is unimpressed.
There is no event loop running. You skipped a step.
This needs an event loop and you brought none.
asyncio looked around for a loop to run in and found silence.
You forgot to actually start the async machinery before using it.
RuntimeError: the loop you assumed was running was never running.

fix.summary: Run the coroutine with asyncio.run() or from within an active event loop.

title: TypeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute
jokes: Something returned None, and then you asked it for '.{attr_name}' anyway.
'.{attr_name}' on None: the most Python error of all Python errors.
You assumed that function would return something. It returned nothing, as promised by no one.
None does not have '.{attr_name}'. None does not have anything.
This is what happens when a function silently returns None and you don't check.
'.{attr_name}' of NoneType: the sequel nobody asked for, again.

fix.summary: Trace back where the value became None and add a check before accessing it.

title: StopIteration
jokes: You called next() one too many times. The iterator has nothing left to give.
StopIteration: the iterator's polite way of saying it's done.
This generator is exhausted, much like you are right now.
You kept asking for more, but the iterator already told you it was empty.
next() past the end of an iterator. There was never going to be a happy ending here.
The well is dry. So is this iterator.

fix.summary: Catch StopIteration or use a for loop / default value with next() instead.

title: OSError: Address already in use
jokes: Something else is already bound to that address. Probably your last unkilled process.
OSError: this address is already spoken for.
You started this server twice and forgot about the first one.
Address already in use: the socket equivalent of someone else's stuff in your seat.
This port has a tenant, and it isn't moving out on its own.
You need to evict whatever is already listening there.

fix.summary: Find and stop the process already bound to that port, or use a different one.

title: pytest: error collecting test module
jokes: pytest couldn't even load your test file, let alone run it.
This test module failed before a single test got the chance to fail properly.
Collection error: pytest gave up before the real disappointment could begin.
Your test file has a bug in it. The tests haven't even started yet.
pytest tried to import your test module and it fell apart immediately.
This is a bad import inside a test file, not a failing test. Different problem, same energy.

fix.summary: Check the traceback for an import error or syntax error in the test file itself.

title: UnicodeDecodeError
jokes: This file isn't the encoding you assumed it was. It never was.
UnicodeDecodeError: bytes and your assumed charset are not on speaking terms.
You told Python this was UTF-8. Python disagrees, loudly.
Somewhere out there is a file saved in an encoding from 2003.
This is what happens when you don't specify an encoding and hope for the best.
The bytes are real. Your assumption about what they mean is not.

fix.summary: Open the file with the correct encoding, or detect it before reading.

title: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s)

matcher.pattern: TypeError: unsupported operand type\(s\) for \+: '(\w+)' and '(\w+)'

jokes: You can't add a '{left_type}' and a '{right_type}'. Math has rules.
'{left_type}' + '{right_type}' is not defined, and neither is your type discipline.
This is what happens when you assume everything is secretly a string. Or a number. Whichever it wasn't.
Python refuses to guess how to combine a '{left_type}' and a '{right_type}'.
You mixed types like a smoothie and Python is not blending.
'{left_type}' and '{right_type}' were never meant to be added together.

fix.summary: Convert both operands to a common type before combining them.

title: json.decoder.JSONDecodeError
jokes: That string is not JSON. It just kind of looks like it.
json.loads() met your input and immediately regretted it.
Whatever you're parsing is not valid JSON, no matter how much you want it to be.
This is what happens when an API returns HTML for an error and you parse it as JSON anyway.
The JSON parser choked. Probably on a trailing comma or an empty response.
Somewhere in that payload is a syntax mistake, or it's just not JSON at all.

fix.summary: Print the raw response/string before parsing to see what was actually returned.

title: ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package

matcher.pattern: ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package

jokes: You ran a module directly that expected to be part of a package. It wasn't.
Relative imports need a package structure, and you just ran a lone script.
This file doesn't know it's supposed to be part of something bigger.
You used a dot-import outside of any package context. Python has no idea what you meant.
Running this file directly broke the illusion that it was ever a package member.
Relative imports work great, right up until you run the file standalone.

fix.summary: Run the module with -m from the package root instead of executing the file directly.

title: UnboundLocalError

matcher.pattern: UnboundLocalError: local variable '(\w+)' referenced before assignment

jokes: '{name}' is local, and you used it before it had a value. Scoping strikes again.
You assigned to '{name}' somewhere in this function, which made Python treat it as local everywhere.
'{name}' exists, but not yet, not here, not like this.
This is the classic 'assigned later in the function so it shadows the outer scope' bug.
'{name}' was referenced before assignment because Python decided it was local the moment you touched it anywhere.
You wanted the global '{name}'. Python gave you scoping rules instead.

fix.summary: Use the global/nonlocal keyword, or rename the local variable to avoid shadowing.

title: AssertionError
jokes: You asserted something that wasn't true. The assertion was right to complain.
AssertionError: reality did not match your expectations.
This assert statement caught exactly what it was written to catch. Working as intended.
Your assumption failed its own test.
The code checked itself and did not like what it found.
assert is doing its job. Your logic is the one that failed.

fix.summary: Check the condition being asserted and the actual value at that point.

title: MemoryError
jokes: You asked Python to hold more than the machine has to give.
MemoryError: you built something enormous and the RAM said enough.
This is what happens when you load the entire dataset into memory at once.
Your process just asked for more memory than exists. Bold request.
The machine ran out of RAM trying to satisfy your data structure.
This was always going to happen eventually. Today was the day.

fix.summary: Process the data in chunks/streams instead of loading it all into memory.

title: BrokenPipeError
jokes: The other end of this pipe hung up, and you kept writing to it anyway.
BrokenPipeError: nobody is listening on the other side anymore.
You piped output to something that closed early. It happens.
The reader left. The writer did not get the memo.
This is what happens when you `| head` a program that keeps producing output.
The pipe is broken because the process on the other end quit without telling you.

fix.summary: Handle the broken pipe gracefully, or check why the downstream process exited early.

title: ImportError: cannot import name from module (version mismatch)
jokes: '{name}' doesn't exist in the '{module_name}' you actually have installed.
You're expecting an API from '{module_name}' that a different version provides.
'{name}' was removed, renamed, or never existed in this version of '{module_name}'.
This is what happens when your requirements.txt and reality disagree on versions.
Somewhere between the docs you read and the package you installed, '{name}' vanished.
'{module_name}' changed its API and nobody told this codebase.

fix.summary: Check the installed version of the package matches what the code expects.
